To enfranchise means to grant someone a right, freedom, or power that they were previously denied. It is about letting people in — into a system, a process, or a society — after they had been locked out of it.

Think of it this way: imagine a room where important decisions are made. Some people are allowed inside; others are kept at the door. To enfranchise someone is to open that door for them and say, "You belong here too."
The Most Common and Specific Meaning — The Right to Vote

In everyday use, enfranchise almost always refers to granting the right to vote. When a government enfranchises a group of people, it officially gives them the legal right to participate in elections — something they could not do before.

For example:

  • The 19th Amendment to the U.S. Constitution enfranchised women in 1920, meaning women gained the right to vote for the first time.
  • For centuries, poor people who didn't own land were not enfranchised — they had no say in who governed them.
  • Many civil rights movements throughout history fought to enfranchise Black citizens, Indigenous people, and other groups who were deliberately excluded from voting.

So when you see or hear "enfranchise" in a political or historical context, it almost certainly means: giving someone the right to vote.
The Broader Meaning — General Freedom and Empowerment

Beyond voting, enfranchise is also used more broadly to mean giving someone the freedom, power, or means to participate fully in something — to have a real voice, a real stake, a real place.

In this wider sense, it means removing whatever barrier was keeping someone powerless or excluded.

For example:

  • A company that gives its employees a role in decision-making is enfranchising its workers — it is giving them a genuine voice rather than just taking orders.
  • Access to quality education can enfranchise people from poor backgrounds by equipping them to engage with opportunities that were previously out of reach.
  • A new law that allows people with disabilities to access public spaces more easily enfranchises them — it brings them into full participation in society.

In all these cases, the idea is the same: someone who was excluded, overlooked, or powerless is now being given access, rights, or real influence.
The Historical Meaning — Freedom from Slavery or Bondage

In older and historical texts, enfranchise was used to mean setting someone free from slavery, serfdom, or other forms of bondage. A slave who was formally freed, or a serf released from obligation to a lord, was said to be enfranchised.

This meaning is rarely used in modern English, but you may encounter it when reading historical documents or literature from earlier centuries.
One More Historical Usage — Towns and Boroughs

In British political history, enfranchise was also used to mean granting a town or borough the right to send elected representatives to Parliament. Just as a person could be enfranchised, so could a place — meaning it was brought into the political system for the first time.

Again, this is historical and specific, and you are unlikely to encounter it in modern conversation, but it is worth knowing.

Every time you see enfranchise, keep its opposite in mind: disenfranchise (sometimes written as disfranchise).

To disenfranchise someone is to take away their rights — especially their right to vote — or to make them feel so powerless and excluded that their participation becomes meaningless even if technically permitted.

For example:

  • Voter suppression tactics disenfranchise communities by making it harder for them to cast their votes.
  • A government that ignores its citizens completely disenfranchises them — their voices count for nothing in practice.

The two words are mirror images of each other: enfranchise opens the door, disenfranchise shuts it.
How the Word is Used in Practice

A few things to note about how this word behaves in sentences:

It is a formal word. You will mostly see and hear it in political writing, journalism, history, law, and serious social commentary. It is not casual conversation language.

It often appears in the passive voice. Rather than saying "The government enfranchised women," people very commonly say "Women were enfranchised in 1920." Both are correct, and you should be comfortable reading both forms.

It always implies a power relationship. There is always someone granting the right and someone receiving it. Enfranchisement is given by those in authority — a government, an institution, a system — to those who had been excluded from it. The people being enfranchised could not simply give themselves this status; it required formal recognition.

It implies previous exclusion. You do not enfranchise someone who already had rights. The word only makes sense when there was a previous state of being shut out.

If you want one clean summary to anchor everything:

To enfranchise is to formally grant someone — especially a group that was previously excluded — the right to participate in a process or system. Most commonly, this means the right to vote. More broadly, it means giving someone genuine freedom, power, or a real voice where they had none before. Its opposite is disenfranchise — to take those rights away, or to render someone's participation meaningless.

The word carries weight. It belongs to serious conversations about justice, power, and who gets to have a say in the world around them.
